mainEntity.name: How is TDEE different from BMR?

acceptedAnswer.text: BMR is calories burned at complete rest. TDEE adds in activity, exercise, and digestion to estimate your true total daily calorie burn.

mainEntity.name: Which BMR formula should I use?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mifflin-St Jeor is the usual default for adults. If you know your body-fat percentage — especially if you're very lean or muscular — Katch-McArdle or Cunningham can be more accurate because they are based on lean body mass.

mainEntity.name: Is the macro split shown here right for everyone?

acceptedAnswer.text: It's a reasonable general-purpose starting point, but optimal macro splits vary by goal (muscle gain, endurance, fat loss) and individual preference.

mainEntity.name: How often should I recalculate my TDEE?

acceptedAnswer.text: Recalculate whenever your weight changes significantly (every 10-15 lbs) or if your activity level changes meaningfully, since TDEE shifts as your body composition and lifestyle change.

mainEntity.name: Why is my actual weight trend different from what my TDEE predicts?

acceptedAnswer.text: Formula-based TDEE is an estimate — actual metabolism varies by individual, so it's normal to need to adjust your calorie target up or down after a few weeks of real-world tracking.

mainEntity.name: How much of a calorie deficit should I use for fat loss?

acceptedAnswer.text: A moderate deficit of roughly 15-25% below TDEE is generally more sustainable and better preserves muscle mass than a very aggressive deficit.
